summary.text: Fermat's little theorem says that if p is a prime and a is a whole number that p does not divide, then aᵖ⁻¹ − 1 is divisible by p.
For example, with a = 2 and p = 7, 2⁶ = 64, and 64 − 1 = 63 = 7 × 9.
It is the basis for the Fermat primality test and one of the fundamental results of elementary number theory.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Pierre de Fermat, who stated it in 1640

facts.label: Why 'little'
facts.value: To distinguish it from Fermat's Last Theorem

facts.label: First pseudoprime found
facts.value: 341, found in 1820 by Pierre Frédéric Sarrus

items.prompt: Take p = 7 and a = 2. Work out 2⁶ − 1. What do you find?

options.label: The result is 63, a multiple of 7
The result is 64, a multiple of 7
The result is 63, which 7 does not divide
The result is 127, a multiple of 7

items.prompt: For the prime 7, which choice of a is ruled out by the theorem's condition?

options.label: Any even number
Any multiple of 7
Any number smaller than 7
Any odd number

items.explain: The theorem requires that p does not divide a, so multiples of 7 are excluded.

items.prompt: A number passes a Fermat-style check for the base 2. A student declares it must be prime. Why is that wrong?

options.label: The check only works for even numbers
The check never works for large numbers
Some composite numbers pass, such as 341 = 11 × 31
Passing proves it is a multiple of 2

items.explain: The 'only if' direction fails: 341 passes for base 2 but is composite, so it is called a pseudoprime.

items.prompt: Fermat has another famous theorem. Why is this one called 'little'?

options.label: It is simpler to state than every other theorem
It was found when Fermat was young
It only works for small numbers
To tell it apart from Fermat's Last Theorem

items.explain: The name distinguishes it from Fermat's Last Theorem.

items.prompt: Euler's theorem uses a count of the whole numbers from 1 to n that share no factor with n. Why does Fermat's little theorem fit inside it?

options.label: When n is prime, that count equals n − 1
When n is prime, that count equals n
When n is even, that count equals 1
Fermat's theorem works for every n

items.explain: For a prime n, every smaller positive number shares no factor with it, so the count is n − 1, and Euler's theorem becomes Fermat's.

items.prompt: What practical use does the theorem have when checking whether a number is prime?

options.label: It lists every prime below the number
It splits the number into its factors
It is the basis for the Fermat primality test
It tells you the number's digits

items.explain: Fermat's little theorem is the basis for the Fermat primality test.
